1: But Christianity takes that notion and modifies it in a fascinating and consequential way: Whereas Romans understand lamiae as people—not demons or gods—but nevertheless as autonomously powerful, Christianity drains the autonomous power out of the Monstrous Bitch.
2: In Revelation, the Whore of Babylon is decisively defeated by the Lord. The threat that she poses to society is obliterated by a single, male, patriarchal divinity. Just as Tiamat is destroyed by Marduk, so the Whore of Babylon is destroyed by Jesus.
3: That is, through allegorical interpretations of these passages, Christian biblical commentators dismantle the realness of the Monstrous Bitches. Lamiae aren’t real monsters, witches, or demonesses anymore. They are instead allegorical figurations for threats to the church.
4: This ideological reason is the Virgin Mary. Mary’s power resides not in her strength, her cunning, her magic, her violence, her ability to summon the dead, her bitchlikeness, or her snakiness but, quite the opposite, in her gentleness, her mercy, her nurturance, and her capacity for self-sacrifice.
5: First, lamiae kill babies; Mary gives birth to a baby and cares for him tenderly—and not just any baby, but the most important baby in human history, the baby through whom all other babies (and indeed all other humans) can be saved from eternal perdition.
6: Lamashtu sneaks into houses at night to kill babies; Mary sneaks into a manger to deliver and cherish one. Lamiae’s murderousness is meant to stymie mankind; Mary’s tenderness toward her baby is meant to bring about mankind’s salvation.
7: Lamia gets enraged and violent after the death of her children; Mary mourns but accepts the death of her child and then turns around to offer succor to those whom he had loved.
8: Mary, on the other hand, is quiet—even at the Crucifixion of her only child: she may talk, and she may weep, but she is never crazed, frantic, or dysregulated. She certainly never curses anyone. Really and truly, Mary is the antithesis of Lamashtu, or Lamia, or Medea, or any of the other Greco-Roman witch-bitches out there.
9: Christian witches—unlike Roman witches or Greek ones—were vehicles for evil, not evil itself. There was no room for the ideology of the autonomous lamia, because any magic-practicing evildoer was, by definition, an employee of Satan, possessed by and acting out his evil will.
